Because Nike was. Nike built its golf clubs in a facility in Fort Worth and exited the equipment business in 2016, which released a building and a group of experienced club builders into the same city. Artisan Golf was founded by two former Nike craftsmen, Mike Taylor and John Hatfield, in February 2017 and works out of the former Nike golf club facility. P53's Christopher Griffin leases space at Leonard Golf Links, in the building Nike used, from Marty Leonard — daughter of Marvin Leonard, who founded Colonial.

Artisan grinds and finishes every club in Fort Worth. Edel hand-finishes its putters in Austin. P53 forges in the Pacific Northwest but does all machining, grinding and finishing in Fort Worth. On the apparel side it is mostly design here, sewing elsewhere — Criquet prints made in Peru on the Top-Shelf Players Shirt, and Sierra Madre's All Square Skort is Peruvian cotton.

Mike Taylor and John Hatfield, both former Nike employees. Hatfield has given the exact date: February 17, 2017 was their last day on the Nike payroll, and on Monday February 20 they walked in the same door and started Artisan. Taylor was Nike's model maker for irons and wedges; Hatfield built putters. Wedges are ground by Taylor personally and can only be ordered after an in-person fitting in Fort Worth.

aug-11.name: Aug 11
src: Aug 11 isn't a golf brand. It's a hat brand. But the best hats on the course right now aren't coming from golf companies — they're crossing over from streetwear, from lifestyle, from places where fit and story matter more than a logo on a divot tool. Aug 11 is that brand.

Before you dismiss it as another DTC hat company, look at who's wearing them. Aaron Judge. Jrue Holiday. Dom Dolla wore Aug 11 to three of his four Coachella sets. Adam Mosseri — the head of Instagram — posted in one to his 2.4 million followers. None of that was paid. The hats just fit well and look right, and people with platforms noticed.

beams-golf.name: BEAMS Golf
src: In 1976, a guy named Etsuzo Shitara opened a 21.5 square meter shop in Harajuku called American Life Shop BEAMS. Styled like a UCLA dorm room, stocked with early Nike running sneakers and West Coast campus wear his partner bought on trips to California with enormous empty bags. Fifty years later, BEAMS operates 160 stores with 50 sub-labels and is considered, in Nigo's words, the very pinnacle of Tokyo culture. In 2011, they turned that editorial eye to golf — and created Japan's first select-shop golf brand.

The man behind it is Satoshi Nishiwaki, who joined BEAMS as a part-timer in 1995 and had never played golf before directing the brand. That turned out to be the point. BEAMS Golf doesn't start from performance and add style. It starts from fashion identity and engineers performance into it. Three sub-labels cover the range: Orange Label for American-casual boldness, Purple Label for modernized tradition, and B.G.THREE for minimalist city-to-course crossover. In 2019, a 20-year-old rookie named Hinako Shibuno wore BEAMS Golf Orange Label to win the AIG Women's British Open — her first tournament outside Japan. The polo sold out within hours. BEAMS issued a victory commemorative edition four days later.

The collaboration list reads like a who's-who of taste: Malbon Golf, Polo Ralph Lauren, BRIEFING, Hender Scheme, SON OF THE CHEESE, Nike Golf, Jones Sports Co . Fifteen collaborations deep with Ralph Lauren alone. The catch is getting it stateside — BEAMS ships internationally through WorldShopping, Buyee handles proxy orders, and the occasional Malbon or FARFETCH drop crosses the Pacific. That barrier is part of the appeal. You won't see it at the local muni. You'll know who did their homework.

Leather was the standard before rubber won on price and durability, and BestGrips has been making them by hand in Conroe, Texas since 2003. Leather moves under the hand differently to rubber and it patinas with use. It also costs more and wants more care.

src: Bluegrass Fairway is a small workshop in Louisville, Kentucky making leather, Harris Tweed and waxed canvas golf goods by hand — headcovers, yardage book covers, valuables pouches, rangefinder cases and the occasional needlepoint belt. Around 172 products are live at any one time, priced from about $38 for a hat to $1,100 for a bag built out of a repurposed Barbour jacket.

Reynolds grew up in Louisville and took his first job at Wildwood Country Club. He became a scratch player and finished inside the top five at the Kentucky Open. When Bluegrass Fairway started he was working at his family's insurance agency, and had been since he was twenty-two. I work at my family's insurance agency and have since I was 22 years old, so the Bluegrass Fairway thing is kind of a side project for me, he told GolfWRX in October 2017. Whether that is still true is not something the brand has said publicly since.

A little. Around 28 products are Bluegrass Fairway apparel produced by partners — the Tour Visor is made by Holderness & Bourne — and a Vintage Pro Shop collection of about nine items launched in May 2026, selling secondhand and new-old-stock golf clothing under the labels "Gently Used," "New Old Stock" and "New." The other 135 products are their own.

Six of the eighteen were sold out at the time of writing: Mogshade Parmore, Birds of Condor, Radry Golf, Sugarloaf Social Club, Bluegrass Fairway and Left of Field. All six are repeat items their brands have restocked before.

bluetross.name: Bluetross
src: One pattern turns up again and again. Megan Chisti co-founded Seamus, trained as the designer, rebuilt the headcover that started the company and still sews product, and there is no published quote from her anywhere. Gail Hanson co-founded Bluetross, and the first prototypes came off her inherited sewing machine; the biggest feature ever written about the company is headlined the unlikely story of a man who quit his job to make leather headcovers. Neither brand is hiding anything, and both credit her plainly on their own About page. The voice just defaults to him. So every entry names the woman, and says plainly when she co-founded with a husband or a mother rather than rounding up.

casualist.name: Casualist
src: The best-selling item Casualist makes has the wrong name on it. The Casual Pro Snapback is the oldest thing in the catalogue, it restocked this month, and stitched across the front is CASUAL PRO, SINCE 2023, LEISURE APPAREL, MELB LDN LA. That was the brand before this one.

Elie Reboul renamed it. His explanation, on the about page, is two sentences long: the spirit was right, but the name needed to grow up a little. What he did not do is retire the old hat, and the archive section still sells a navy coach jacket with CASUAL PRO in block type across the back.

src: Cloud & Wind Golf is a grip brand that makes one thing and makes it differently. Every design draws from traditional Eastern aesthetics and Pacific Coast nature — floral Blossom motifs, twilight Cloud & Wave colorways, stripped-back Zen textures — with a line of Chinese verse printed along each shaft.

In the brand's own words, 'We dig back into our heritage and look for inspiration.' Cloud & Wind Golf brings traditional Eastern design elements into the golf bag — inspired by nature, rooted in heritage, and crafted with passion. Rather than chase logos, the team builds grips around a feeling: capturing the beauty of the course so you can carry it in your hands.

Several tops carry 39 RUE MADAME PARIS across the back — A.P.C.'s head office in the 6th, with its Paris store across the road at 38 — transplanted onto Japanese golf wear. The half zip goes one better and runs that address against Cph/Golf's own house line, NOT A GOLF GENTLEMAN . Six tops and one jacket, all cut with the roomy shoulder and slightly cropped body Cph/Golf uses across its own range. Every reference is sized M to XL against a 183cm fit model in L, so the cm charts matter more than the letter.

Cph/Golf's store is set up as a Japanese market and nothing else. The shipping policy is written entirely for domestic delivery — business days, remote-island timing — and there is no international checkout to find. So there are two indirect routes, and both cost more than the sticker.

A collaboration between A.P.C. Golf, the golf line of the Paris label A.P.C., and Cph/Golf, the golf line of the Tokyo streetwear brand CAPTAINS HELM. The name fuses both marks into one — A.P.Cph — and it appears on the chest of nearly every piece. It released on September 2, 2026 as 18 references: 11 men's and unisex, 7 women's.

Not directly. Cph/Golf's webstore is configured as a Japan-only market and its shipping policy covers domestic delivery, down to noting delays to Japan's remote islands. The routes that exist are a proxy service that buys on your behalf, or a forwarding service that gives you a Japanese address to ship to — both add cost and neither is guaranteed for an independent Shopify store.

criquet.name: Criquet Shirts
src: Criquet makes golf shirts that never announce themselves as golf shirts, which is how the same four-button placket ends up on a Butler tee box and at a South Congress bar three hours later. Billy Nachman and Hobson Brown have known each other since kindergarten in Manhattan, where they grew up in prep-school polos and coat-and-tie dress codes, and they started the company in Austin in 2010. It begins in a closet, with the vintage golf shirt Nachman's grandfather left behind: four buttons, a long placket, a collar that had opinions. They rebuilt it with a flap chest pocket, removable collar stays so the collar never bacons at the tip, and an organic-cotton pitch that was ahead of its time, and called it the Players Shirt. It runs in 100 per cent Peruvian pima today and still costs ninety-eight dollars.

The name comes from the sound of crickets, by the brand's own telling: the noise of being comfortably off-course. Criquet has never fully committed to being a golf brand. One half of the catalogue is Range Polos in brrr , a mineral-infused yarn that moves heat off the skin, and Players Shirts you could tee off in at Butler. The other half runs pearl snaps, fine-wale corduroy in burnt orange and a loop-terry shirt called Midnight Toker, which belongs on a pool deck more than a first tee. The two halves hang in the same closet.

Criquet is an Austin company in a way that shows up in the product. The longtime clubhouse-headquarters on South First had a putting green, an outdoor bar and a Bill Murray mural. The collaboration list reads like a city directory: Zilker Belts from across the river, YETI from fifteen minutes up the road, the home team Austin FC under an official MLS license, and a Willie Nelson Willie Forever collection that has since been delisted. Discmania, the Finnish house that supplies most of disc golf, printed the brand's mascot Carl onto a three-disc set. The store currently carries a belt strap in Save Muny colors and a tee with a Lions badge, which is more Lions Municipal product than some golf labels carry product at all.

Six live collabs $45 to $150 Criquet collaborates the way Austin institutions do, which is locally first. Zilker Belts and YETI are neighbors, Austin FC is the home team, and Jones and Discmania make up the out-of-state guest list.

Billy Nachman and Hobson Brown, friends since kindergarten in Manhattan who grew up in prep-school polos and coat-and-tie dress codes. They founded Criquet in Austin in 2010, after Nachman found his late grandfather's vintage four-button golf shirt in a closet and the pair decided to rebuild it properly.

Austin, Texas — the brand has said it plainly since day one: "We founded Criquet here in 2010." Its longtime clubhouse-headquarters sat at 1603 South 1st Street in Bouldin Creek, complete with a putting green, an outdoor bar and a Bill Murray mural.

devereux-golf.name: Devereux Golf
src: What's striking about going back to that interview is how little the technical brief has moved. Robert named three details then that Devereux is still building around now: a slightly smaller spread collar that stays out of the way through the swing, a placket thinned down so it lies flat, and a fit shaped around how men are actually built. Add a smaller chest pocket and you have described the Homestead and the Phoenician, twelve years later.

The part that did change is the artwork. Devereux rebranded in 2021 toward a younger golfer, and somewhere in there it stopped being a contemporary-fit polo company and became a Southwestern graphics house that also makes polos. The current run is eagles, sunbursts, scorpions, motorcycles, pin-up girls, Our Lady of Guadalupe, and an invented club called the Pioneer Country Club rendered as a neon sign. It's tattoo flash and old highway signage, and it is doing something nobody else in golf is doing.

The headcovers are where that lands hardest. They're leather, they're $54, and the embroidery is dense enough to survive a macro shot. That is a real test, and most embroidered golf product fails it. If you only ever buy one Devereux thing, buy a cover.

Below is everything new since we first wrote about them: outerwear, polos, shorts, headcovers, hats, tees and accessories. One thing to flag: Devereux doesn't currently make pants or joggers. Shorts are the only bottoms in the line.
Where Devereux gets least loud and most useful. The jackets are cut closer to a work coat than a golf shell, and most of them read fine off the course.
No pants or joggers in the current run. Shorts are the only bottoms Devereux makes, and two of them earn a spot in the bag.

src: Students Golf 's Draft Blade is the $50 entry point — clean, magnetic, Texas-made. Small-batch, made by people who care about leather, lining, and the snap of a magnetic closure. $50 to $150, all personality.

Eleven putter covers from eleven brands, and every one of them has more personality than the putter it's protecting. Birds of Condor 's Tokyo Country Club blade cover channels Japanese minimalism at $69.95. Dormie Workshop's 3 Wishes Mallet Cover at $155 is handcrafted leather you'll be nervous to actually use. eastside-golf.name: Eastside Golf
src: Eastside Golf's Core Fleece Swingman sets the tone at ~$88 — premium cotton, Swingman embroidery, streetwear DNA. From there, Gumtree Golf goes heavyweight at $145, Malbon pushes into the $185 range with the Safety Buckets Fesque, and Casualist keeps it understated at ~$85. Brands like Sounder, Sugarloaf Social Club , and Jones Golf Bags fill the middle. Whether you need a layer for early morning tee times or a post-round pullover that doesn't scream "I just played 18," the edit covers it.

The range here is the point. You've got Whim Golf's $309 merino long sleeve sitting next to Devereux's $74 Back9 Polo, and both make sense. Eastside Golf, Quiet Golf , Birds of Condor , Sugarloaf , Metalwood, Greyson, UNRL — each one doing their own thing, none of them copying each other. Summer sorted.

We pulled 18 gloves across both worlds. The range runs from the $10 Callaway Dawn Patrol — full leather at a price that shouldn't be possible — to the $48 Malbon Buckets Glove, where Fairfax Ave streetwear meets the first tee. In between: Ghost Golf's stealthy premium Cabretta, Pins & Aces' Colorado-born prints, Eastside Golf's culturally charged Swingman, Vivantee's NYC-inspired designs, and the cult-favorite Asher Evergreen in every color you didn't know you needed.

The lineup opens with Metalwood Studio 's adidas MC70 — a Predator upper on a golf chassis — and runs through Quiet Golf 's Samba, Eastside Golf's Jordan AJ1 Low, Malbon's in-house Tour 1, and three Nike retros that belong on a course as much as they do on concrete. PAYNTR shows up three times through collabs with Students Golf , Sugarloaf Social Club , and Vessel — each one engineered differently, each one carrying a different brand's DNA. Thirteen shoes, thirteen stories, $125 to $250.

Jordan's spring '26 golf lineup is stacked. The AJ1 Low Golf "Chicago" spiked drops May 10 at $175, the White/Fir Augusta colorway landed April 1, and Eastside Golf's ADG 4 is still the culture play. Tony Finau, Mookie Betts, and Chris Paul are all in the campaign.

This is 18 picks from 18 brands across jackets, pants, hats, umbrellas, and bag covers. The range runs from a $20 Stitch Golf snap-on rain hood to Manors Golf 's 2.5L Pertex WP Jacket — the highest waterproof rating on this list. In between: Eastside Golf's culture-forward Script Umbrella, Birds of Condor 's recycled ripstop all-weather jacket from Australia, a Jones Sports Co . rain hood towel that's the smartest dual-purpose accessory in golf, and a Galvin Green GORE-TEX jacket on sale for $233 that's usually $389. Every category, every price tier, all from brands doing their own thing.

edel-golf.name: Edel Golf
src: Artisan grinds and finishes every club in Fort Worth. Edel hand-finishes its putters in Austin. P53 forges in the Pacific Northwest but does all machining, grinding and finishing in Fort Worth. Piretti mills in the United States. Lamb Crafted machines in Plano. BestGrips states designed and made in Texas. Clint Orms engraves by hand in Texas. On the apparel side it is mostly design here, sewing elsewhere — Criquet prints made in Peru on the Top-Shelf Players Shirt, and Sierra Madre's All Square Skort is Peruvian cotton.

In Austin. Edel's own product pages state it plainly: The Brick is precision-milled in the U.S.A. from premium stainless steel and hand-finished in Austin, Texas, and the E-T01 is machined in the U.S.A. from premium carbon steel then hand-painted and assembled in Austin. Their wording is that each head is individually painted, polished and built by their master craftsmen. The brand was founded by David Edel and is known for fitting putters the way most fitters approach irons.

Milled versus stamped. A stamped tool is cut and pressed from sheet; a milled one is machined from solid billet. Milled prongs hold their geometry and resist rolling over at the tip, which is what turns a cheap tool into a bent one. Edel mills, Kraken mills, Gamut casts in brass. The $20 pieces are stamped, and at that price that is a fair exchange.

For $19.99 the Frogger HOP! opens one-handed and lives on a bag clip. For a tool you will keep, the Edel Fine Milled at $45 is milled rather than stamped. If you want something hand-made, Seamus forges its single-prong Greenskeeper in Portland at $76.

It also runs through a lot of drop-down menus. Only a handful of these makers do one-off work: Show Out and the other independent engravers, Artisan in Fort Worth, KYOEI's custom programme, and Anthony Taranto, whose wedges are not for sale. Grindworks, Fourteen, Bettinardi, Edel, New Level, Indi and Miura all label their wedges custom, and all of them mean built-to-order from a fixed set of options. Built-to-order is a good way to buy a wedge, but it is not bespoke, and the word custom covers both without telling you which one you are getting.

edison-golf.name: Edison Golf
src: Several, and in more categories than people expect. Clubs and metal: Artisan Golf and P53 in Fort Worth, Piretti in Spring, Edison Golf in Rockport, Lamb Crafted in Plano. Leather and silver: BestGrips in Conroe, Chipp Golf Co in Dallas, Clint Orms in Kerrville. Apparel: Criquet and Sierra Madre in Austin, Olydoe and Kingfisher in Dallas, Juniper & James in New Braunfels. Individual makers: AustinKnittyLimits and Ally Aiken Design, both in Austin.

ekorre-golf.name: Ekorre Golf
src: Ash. ScotSticks makes the case that ash was golf's original wood before hickory crossed from America, and cuts its sticks from it in Scotland. Ekorre goes further and laminates six strips of Swedish ash into a hexagon, the way a split-cane fishing rod is made, so the stick flexes and returns straight.

The details that differ. Length runs 42 to 45 inches; Hickory & Heath picked 43 so the sticks sit below the woods in the bag. Ends are either capped — bronze at Scotch & Skins, brass at Hazy, tack caps at Beavertail, nail caps at BubbaWhips — or bare and chamfered, as ScotSticks and Ekorre prefer. Almost everyone engraves, and about half will paint your colours to order.

The makers here select straight-grained hickory, ash or walnut and most seal it against moisture; Ekorre laminates six strips of ash into a hexagon specifically so the stick returns to straight after flexing. Wood will always move a little more than a fiberglass rod, which is why several shops advise keeping the sticks out of a wet bag.

BubbaWhips (builder), Hickory & Heath (colours, stripe design, engraving), Beavertail (custom design plus free names), Nor'easter (its main line is fully custom; the ACK-ley is the stock pair), Thwack (Pick Your Own Hickory Switch, $139), Out West (engraving) and Ekorre (custom colours and a name for a fee).

Because they are made and sold from there. ScotSticks lists at 51 and ships worldwide with a three-week lead; Ekorre lists at 2,400 kr from Sigtuna. Both note that import duties outside their region are paid by the buyer, so the dollar figures in this post are approximate.

evnroll.name: Evnroll
src: Mizuno's M.Craft City Series at $350 is the value play. Swag Golf's Handsome One at $400 is the culture play. Evnroll's ER2 Origin and LA Golf's Bel-Air X round out a lineup where every option has a real argument behind it. If you've been rolling with the same putter since 2019, this is the year that changes.

fella-golf.name: Fella Golf
src: Fella Golf is an Amsterdam-based label registered as Fella Golf B.V. and built on a single line: "for the ones already too far gone. It only takes one good shot." That slogan runs through everything they make — from rib knit polos and cashmere vests to pizza-themed headcovers and ball markers stamped with the motto. The S/S '26 collection just dropped, and it covers the full spectrum: polos, tees, knitwear, outerwear, headwear, bags, and playful accessories that refuse to take the game too seriously.

What sets Fella apart is the range. A 190 cotton-cashmere golf cart intarsia crewneck sits next to a 15 golden pizza slice ball marker. A limited collab with Portland's Jones Sports Co on bags shares shelf space with a "Sandbagger" graphic tee and a bucket hat called the Cha-Cheng. The brand transcends golf from course to everyday wear — streetwear boldness meets traditional golf aesthetics, Dutch design meets global ambition. If you've been looking for the European answer to the indie golf wave, Fella is already too far gone.

forden-golf.name: Forden Golf
src: Forden Golf makes clothes for municipal golf, and it is specific about it. The graphics are in-jokes about the local muni, the scorecard and the putt you left short. The cuts are boxy cotton and heavyweight fleece rather than anything technical. The whole range runs from fourteen dollars to seventy-seven. None of it is trying to get you through the gate at a club that would ask what you shot.

The reference points are skate graphics and mid-century sports print, and the logo tells you which one the brand takes seriously. Forden calls the mark the Swingman, and it comes from Harold Edgerton's strobe photography at MIT in 1938: a golfer dissolved into fifty superimposed selves, the shaft still bending after the ball has gone. Flattened to one colour on a hat panel, the figure keeps what made the original work. It is a picture of motion rather than a picture of a golfer.

Chad Gurman founded the brand and has kept the brief narrow. Forden Golf was founded on the belief that golf fashion should be as dynamic and expressive as the game itself. Our mission is to provide a wardrobe that effortlessly blends the elegance of the sport with the boldness of street style, Gurman says on the brand's own site. In practice that means cotton fleece, boxy tees, type-led graphics about municipal golf, and a hat line made with New Era.

What Forden does not have is photography of anyone wearing any of it. There is no lookbook, no on-course imagery, no on-model shots at all; the Gallery page on their site is an empty template. For a brand whose stated business is expression, that is the obvious gap, and it is the one thing holding the range back from reading as clearly as it deserves to. The clothes are better than the pictures of them.

SWING KINGS $14 — Start here, because it is the most Forden object Forden makes. The tee picks come in a foil sachet in Newport green, gold and white stripe across the top, the wordmark set in the same heavy slab a cigarette pack uses, and SWING KINGS printed across the bottom where the format would normally go. The tees inside are wooden and stamped 33. It is a joke that took real work to land, and it is the only thing in the range photographed with any styling at all.

THE LOGO, ON EVERYTHING ELSE — The Swingman mark is a figure mid-swing rendered as overlapping strokes, and it is a direct reference to a photograph. Doc Edgerton fired a strobe a hundred times a second at a golfer at MIT in 1938 and produced a body dissolving into fifty superimposed selves. Forden has flattened that into a logo, and it works hardest on the accessories, where the repeat has room to run.

found-golf.name: Found Golf
src: Melbourne's Found Golf treats the course like a studio and the dress code like a memo it never received. Fashion-first golf from a city that already knows how to blend streetwear with fine art.

The Box Par Tee is the entry point — a heavyweight graphic shirt that reads like an art-school print, not tournament merch. The Daisy Chain Tee runs the same energy. The Reusable Ciggie Box is actually a tee holder, which is the most Found Golf thing imaginable. Dad cap in olive and The Shiz Vest round out a tight five-piece lineup. Everything priced in AUD, shipped from Australia, but the aesthetic is universal: golf gear for people who went to art school.

For clothing: Left of Field Golf out of Sydney, Walker Golf Things on the Gold Coast, Penta on Sydney's Northern Beaches, Gray + Haast in Burleigh Heads, Okka in Perth, Found Golf in Melbourne, Birds of Condor in Byron Bay, and Midiron, which will not tell you where it is based. For leather and wool goods: Mackem Golf in the Perth hills and Big Dog Golf Co. in Victoria, whose covers are stocked in the pro shops at Royal Melbourne, Barnbougle, Royal Adelaide and Cape Wickham. Most price in Australian dollars, though Left of Field and Birds of Condor both run overseas storefronts that will show you a converted price.

The honest range for an organised trip is roughly US$4,250 to US$21,000 per person, and the spread is mostly about how many rounds you get. Pioneer Golf's Tasmania-only package starts around US$4,250 and is the cheapest credible option we found. Random Golf Club is US$6,195 for eight rounds and a scramble. PerryGolf's custom trips start near US$9,415 and their escorted departure runs US$20,995. Watch the round count — Premier Golf's US$4,975 headline buys four rounds across ten days, not the seven you get elsewhere. Airfare from the US is almost never included.

Gumtree Golf's To Fight A Mockingbird is the headliner: a $60 clap-back after Under Armour lifted elements of their design. Students Golf brings two — Grass Obsession and God Knows — both screen-printed in Texas. Malbon runs the Bermuda line. Agronomy Workshop's heavyweight work shirt at $136 barely qualifies as a tee but absolutely qualifies as a statement. Radry, Found Golf , Manors , Birds of Condor , Sugarloaf Social Club — 11 brands, three continents, $28 to $136. Not a dri-fit in sight.

fyfe-golf.name: Fyfe Golf
src: Fyfe Golf makes headcovers to order in a workshop in Fife, out of Harris Tweed, Scottish tartan, waxed canvas from Dundee and, several times a year, something that used to be a completely different object — an RAF flight suit, a caddie's coverall from Augusta, a deck chair, a bolt of sail cloth off a yacht on the west coast. Thirty-two pieces are below, twenty-three of them headcovers, all in stock on 14 September 2026.

The brand started with a complaint. Neil Rennie had spent years walking into Scottish pro shops and finding nothing in them that had anything to do with Scotland. Going around the pro shops and golf retailers, I couldn't find that more elevated product, with heritage and provenance, he told The Wandering Golfers in 2022. Everything was mass-produced and heavily branded. He had come out of fashion rather than golf, which meant he already knew who still wove cloth in Scotland and how to reach them. Fyfe launched in November 2021.

The workshop is a joint venture, not a contractor. Rennie set it up in Fife with what he has called a small group of friends and family, and it is where every headcover is cut, lined and sewn. Fyfe publishes a set of coordinates on its own story page — 56.3438 N, 2.8031 W, which puts you in the East Neuk near Crail — and no street address. Distribution runs from the same county.

Most of it does not exist until you order it. Fyfe describes its approach as producing in response to demand rather than overmaking , which in practice means a custom cover ships in fourteen to twenty-one working days and the standing range is small on purpose. The custom programme has a published price ladder rather than a quote-on-request page: 15 to make an item to order, a further 15 fabric surcharge on one or two covers in a bespoke tartan that is waived at three or more in the same cloth, 20 for initials, 30 setup plus 8.50 per application for custom embroidery. You choose outer fabric, lining, label colour and embroidery.

And they publish an Honesty Box. On the fabrics page Fyfe names the two materials in its own products that are not natural — elastane in the internal grip of a headcover, switched over from organic cotton and rubber because the tension was inconsistent, and polycotton in some linings, chosen over pure organic cotton for strength. Plenty of brands publish a sustainability page. Very few use it to list what they have compromised on and why.

Rennie is the founder and, per Companies House, the sole director of Fyfe Golf Ltd. He has described himself as a co-founder as well, crediting a small group consisting of friends and family without naming them. The company was incorporated on 1 August 2023, two years after the brand launched — there is no predecessor entity on the register, and Fyfe has never explained the gap.

gamut-golf.name: Gamut Golf
src: Gamut Golf makes driver headcovers out of things that already existed. The baseball covers are cut from authentic vintage jerseys, several of them marked 1 of 1. The course covers are cut from genuine course towels — Shinnecock, Pebble Beach, the Old Course, Sawgrass, Pinehurst. Alongside those sit hardwood alignment sticks at $98, a solid brass divot tool, waxed canvas pouches and a set of walnut brushes.

The jerseys. Five covers are cut from authentic baseball jerseys: Cleveland Indians, White Sox, Pittsburgh Pirates, and two Mirage Cooperstown Collection throwbacks — the 1951 New York Giants and the 1957 Milwaukee Braves. Mirage produced officially licensed Cooperstown reissues in the 1990s, so the garments carried licensed marks when they were made. Gamut is cutting finished goods into new ones rather than printing logos, which is a different act entirely. Several are marked 1/1 for the obvious reason: one jersey yields one cover.

No, and they do not need to be. Gamut cuts them from authentic vintage jerseys it has sourced secondhand, including 1990s Mirage Cooperstown Collection throwbacks that were officially licensed when they were manufactured. The covers are upcycled finished garments, not new products bearing printed team marks.

No club partnership is stated by Gamut or discoverable elsewhere. The covers are cut from genuine course towels — real merchandise, repurposed. The Home of Golf cover sidesteps the question by being named for Scotland's Big 4 rather than one club.

Hickory. Nine of the twelve. It was the shaft wood of golf's first two centuries because it is hard, straight-grained and springy, and the makers here mostly buy it as dowel — Scotch & Skins names its supplier, Atlas Dowel & Wood in Ohio — then stain, paint, seal and cap it. It weathers: Gamut says the hickory develops its own character, and that is the point.

garsen-golf.name: Garsen Golf
src: What the independents sell splits two ways. RIPIT and Stick Grips work on the full-swing set and treat the grip as a surface to print on, in limited art series and monogram repeats. The other three work on the putter, where BestGrips wraps cowhide by hand the way grips were made before rubber won on price, Garsen builds a trapezoid nobody else tools up for, and Rosemark moulds a micro-texture that has won ten million dollars on tour.

Five are covered here. RIPIT out of Australia for printed art-series grips at $24.95 and Stick Grips at $13.49 for full-swing sets; BestGrips in Conroe, Texas for handmade leather at $35, Garsen for the trapezoid QUAD at $39.99, and Rosemark for tour-proven micro-texture at $35 on the putter side.

Rosemark is the clearest case: more than ten million dollars won on tour with its grips, and Russell Knox took the 2018 Travelers Championship using the 1.25 MFS. Garsen's QUAD has also been in play on tour.

Rosemark sells into more than twenty-five countries. RIPIT is Australian and ships internationally from there. BestGrips, Stick and Garsen are US-based, so check shipping on the product page before ordering from abroad.

gfore.name: G/FORE
src: This is 18 picks across four categories — hats, shoes, shirts, and accessories — from 18 different brands. The range runs from a $14 Sun Bum face stick to a $195 G/FORE spikeless shoe. In between: a Students Golf Sugarloaf Social Club scout hat built for Texas sun, Manors Golf 's lightweight performance polo from London, Nike ACG trail runners that handle cart paths and fairways, and a $16 Frogg Toggs cooling towel that drops your skin temperature on contact. No polyester boxes from the big-box pro shop. Every pick is from a brand doing something different.

ghost-golf.name: Ghost Golf
src: Jones leads with the 2026 Trouper 4.0 ($315) and the Heritage Trouper ($375) — two different takes on the same obsessive design philosophy. MacKenzie's 8-inch Waxed Canvas Mac ($740) is the heirloom play. Vessel's Lux Stand ($399), Stitch's SL2 Gen 2 ($398), and Shapland's Kantle 3.1 ($490) hold the premium middle. Ghost Golf's Anyday Kovert Ops ($415) rounds it out with a tactical edge. These are the bags people notice on the first tee.

We pulled 18 gloves across both worlds. The range runs from the $10 Callaway Dawn Patrol — full leather at a price that shouldn't be possible — to the $48 Malbon Buckets Glove, where Fairfax Ave streetwear meets the first tee. Anything that moves air. A trucker back, a perforated crown or mesh side panels will all beat solid cotton twill. gramicci.name: Gramicci
src: Gramicci started in 1982 when rock climber Mike Graham needed pants that could handle big-wall climbs without restricting movement. The integrated webbing belt, the gusseted crotch, the freedom-of-movement philosophy — it all started on the granite faces of Yosemite. Forty-plus years later, Gramicci makes everything from the original climbing pant to UPF-rated rashguards, and the brand has quietly become a favorite among golfers who walk munis in the summer heat. The same design principles that work on El Capitan — unrestricted range of motion, durable natural fabrics, easy-adjust fit — work just as well walking 18 in August.

The range runs from the $44 Nylon Gramicci Cap to the $170 Taos Canvas Jacket. Organic cotton twill, nylon-cotton blends with water-repellent finishes, UPF-Shield stretch fabric — Gramicci builds clothes for people who actually move. No logos screaming, no performance marketing jargon, just well-made pieces with real climbing DNA. Eighteen picks here that prove you don't need a golf brand to play great golf.

src: The argument for this group is not who founded the brands but how well the things are made, and Jan Craig is the proof. In 1962 a golfer of that name, out on a rural route outside Cincinnati, made her own headcovers in worsted wool because she could not buy any she liked for a new set of clubs. Jack Nicklaus ordered a set within a few years, Tom Watson carried them, and so did multiple Ryder Cup teams. Every cover is still hand-knit to order, and the only design change in six decades was elastic inside the driver.

jlindeberg.name: J.Lindeberg
src: J.Lindeberg is the brand that made golf clothing fit, and it did it by dressing one Swede in trousers nobody else would wear. The label was founded in Stockholm in 1996 by Johan Lindeberg , who had spent the first half of the nineties building Diesel — first as its distributor in Sweden, later running the American business — and who arrived in golf with a fashion marketer's read on a sport that had stopped caring how it looked. Thirty years on, that founding argument has been so completely absorbed that it is hard to remember it was ever an argument.

Which brings it to Viktor Hovland , who has worn the brand since 2019 and re-signed for three more years in January 2025. His collection is the honest picture of J.Lindeberg now: quieter than the archive, built on technical solids, brown and oxblood and navy, with one colour-blocked polo in it that remembers what this label used to be. Everything below comes from that line, plus the anniversary capsule and a handful of tees.

30 YEARS AND A COLOUR J.Lindeberg is thirty this year and has chosen to celebrate by reselling its own origin story, which is either shameless or exactly right. The capsule is built around one colour and one afternoon in Texas, and the pieces carry the anniversary marks quietly enough that you would have to know what you were looking at.

SIX FROM THE HOVLAND LINE Viktor Hovland has worn J.Lindeberg since 2019 and extended for three more years in January 2025, which makes his collection the clearest statement of what the brand actually wants to be now. It is quieter than the archive suggests. Most of these are plain technical solids, and the one that breaks pattern is the one to look at.

WHERE THE BRAND MADE ITS NAME Trousers are the reason anyone knows this label. The story golf tells about J.Lindeberg is a story about leg width — about a Swede turning up on the range in something cut close when everyone else was swimming in pleated XXXL. The current line is more restrained than that history, but the shapes are still the sharpest part of the range.

OFF-COURSE, MOSTLY The brand runs a serious tee programme because roughly forty per cent of the business is now fashion rather than golf, and the tees are where those two halves meet. None of these read as golf clothing, which is the point — J.Lindeberg has always argued the clothes should work before and after the round as well as during it.

jones-sports-co.name: Jones Sports Co
src: Jones makes the best carry bag in golf by leaving things off it — no legs, no cart strap, no panelling to break the surface — and has been doing that from Portland, Oregon since 1971. The founding story is better than most because it is small. George Jones was a forty-year-old taxi driver who sewed the first bags in his basement and sold them out of the trunk of his cab. Jones still tells it that way on their own history page, and finishes the thought with a line that is hard to improve on: Who could have known? George Jones, that's who.

What their site skips is the middle. George sold the company in 1990, and the new owners tried to make a Jones bag compete with the big manufacturers by making it less like a Jones bag. By the early 2000s the brand was effectively gone. The Lemman family and Chris Carnahan bought it in 2011, and what they bought was almost nothing: no patterns, no inventory, no factory. Matt Lemman, asked later what came with the deal: Just the name, that was all.

The current line runs from the $125 Original through the F-35 ripstop stand bags, the Rider cart bag, eighteen officially licensed school versions and the collaborations with PAYNTR, BEAMS and Lusso Cloud. One correction to something you will read elsewhere: Jones does not claim anywhere on its own site to have invented the single-strap carry bag.

The 1971 Bag, Still Made The Original is the shape everything else came from — 2.9 lbs, three-way divider, unstructured spine. Jones claim only to have been making them since 1971, which is a narrower and more defensible thing to say. Prices run $125 to $215 on material alone.

Where the Patent Lives Jones call their stand system patented and say it remains the gold standard. All of these are built in F-35 recycled ripstop and rated water resistant, from the four-pound Short Course, sized for ten clubs, up to the Utility X and its insulated cooler pocket.

Structured Spine, and the One You Ride With The Players Series is the Original with a structured spine and a two-way divider instead of three, and Jones say the Olive and Sonoma ripstop is woven from 100 PET single-use bottles. The Rider is the only cart bag they make.

kingfisher-golf.name: Kingfisher Golf
src: Kingfisher Golf comes out of Dallas by way of PepsiCo's creative department. Founder Fiona Cohen spent years as an art director specializing in animation and motion design before launching a golf label that treats apparel like a design project — not a merchandise run. The tees are screen-printed at Lewellyn's Print Shop in Old East Dallas. The polos are produced by the same factory teams behind the big-brand performance shirts you already own. Everything stays under $56.

The brand's breakout moment was the Worst Golfer in Dallas contest — a city-wide search for the most entertainingly bad golfer, covered by D Magazine and backed by a cream heavyweight tee that became the brand's fastest seller. The winner, Colin Perry, is now Kingfisher's first sponsored athlete. It's the kind of move that only works when a brand genuinely doesn't take itself too seriously. Heading into the second half of summer, the lineup has grown into a legitimate collection: patterned performance polos, boxy streetwear-cut tees, and a deep hat wall that covers every style from camo trucker to unstructured dad cap. Nothing flashy, nothing over-engineered — just Dallas golf energy with a design eye behind it.

Revisited, August 2026: Kingfisher had a moment this spring — D Magazine covered the "Worst Golfer in Dallas" contest, which ended with Colin Perry crowned as the brand's first sponsored athlete (prize: lessons and general glory). Since our first post, the whole catalog was repriced — polos now $65, tees $40, caps $36 — and the range roughly doubled: the Kit, Mechanic, Navy Zipper, and Cream polos below are new, along with the Golfmobile and Athletics tees and a DAL cap wall that now runs eight colorways deep. Prices updated throughout.
Kingfisher didn't start in a studio. It started at a kitchen counter in East Dallas, at the spot where Fiona usually sat with a sewing machine and a pile of thrift store fabric scraps.

src: Left of Field is the funniest brand in golf that also makes clothes you would wear without the joke attached. Nick Ilias has run it out of Sydney for four years, starting in 2022 in his brother's old bedroom, which he described in a journal entry written in Paris three years later as a small room filled with everything from late-night brainstorming sessions to boxes stacked high with stock.

Royal National Park Royal National Park is Australia's oldest, gazetted in 1879 and running down the coast south of Sydney. Audley is the village at its river crossing and Stanwell sits at its southern edge. The polos carry what Left of Field call an RNP yardage print.

The Short That Made Them Left of Field call the original our answer to everything wrong with golf shorts today — roomy through the trunk, wider at the leg opening, cut to sit just above the knee. It became their best seller, and the 2.0 is a refit of the same idea.

Including Two Very Good Jokes Left of Field run at least five separate marks: a script wordmark, a chainstitched L, a reversed L patch, a flag insignia and a black cockatoo. Two of the caps below are not really about the logo at all.

mackenzie.name: MacKenzie Golf Bags
src: They are unrelated. MacKenzie Golf Bags is named after Rick MacKenzie, a St Andrews caddie. Alister MacKenzie was the golf course architect behind Augusta National, Cypress Point and Royal Melbourne. Products referencing MacKenzie bunkers are referring to the architect, not the bag maker.

In 1985, two brothers from Oregon visited St. Andrews and fell for the simple leather carry bags the Scottish caddies used. They came home and built MacKenzie Golf Bags — handcrafted walkers made one at a time in Portland. Forty years later, Fyfe Golf emerged from Fife, Scotland, making headcovers and accessories from Harris Tweed, tartan, and waxed canvas produced by the Halley Stevenson mill in Dundee — a mill that's been finishing waterproof canvas for North Sea fishermen since 1864. The collaboration was inevitable: Scottish fabric, American leather craft, and a shared obsession with doing one thing well.

Fyfe's longest collaboration is with MacKenzie Golf Bags in Portland, Oregon, and the division of labour is clean: Fyfe supplies the Scottish cloth and designs the colourway and the story, MacKenzie builds the bag. Every edition is a MacKenzie Walker — 8″ opening, single divider, one tartan-lined pocket, full-grain leather, Halley Stevensons waxed canvas, and a leather patch made specifically for that release. They are 650 and they do not last.

Daniel Arsham makes objects look like they've been buried for a thousand years and excavated by mistake. Malbon Golf makes golf look like it belongs in Soho next to Palace and Golf Wang. manors.name: Manors Golf
src: The Honourable Company is Manors' autumn-winter 2026 collection: twenty-two pieces built around merino, Primaloft insulation and Cordura ripstop, priced from a $48 cap to a $305 hooded sweater. It is a layering collection, which is the correct answer to a season where the first tee is cold and the ninth is not.

The name points at the Honourable Company of Edinburgh Golfers, the club that wrote the first surviving rules of golf in 1744. Manors has spent its whole existence borrowing that formal vocabulary — Stableford, Greenskeeper, Ranger, Club — and then cutting the trousers wide and pleated. The collection statement is the brand's own and sets the terms plainly: this is for the Scrambler in every golfer who appreciates good company, great shots and a round wrapped up in less than four hours.

If you play in genuine cold, the mid-layers are the reason to look. If you mostly want golf clothes that do not announce themselves as golf clothes in a bar afterwards, that is the same collection from a different angle — and it is the angle Manors writes to.

One practical note for anyone buying: not everything on the collection page is new. Manors encodes the season in the SKU, and while the AW26 pieces carry an AW26 code, the Ranger Beanie is coded 24AW — a carryover being sold alongside the new collection rather than part of it. The Retro Crown Cap and the Tech Cap use a 26AW code, a different generation of the same season. It is a small thing, but it is the difference between buying this year's collection and buying stock from two winters ago.
Manors is a London brand, founded in 2019 by Charlie Coppola and Jojo Regan, and it sells in dollars to a US audience through its own site. Sizes run XS to XXL across the apparel.

merrill-golf.name: Merrill Golf
src: Merrill Golf calls itself a design venture through the lens of golf, and that's not marketing language — it's a literal description of how the brand operates. No polos. No moisture-wicking polyester. Instead: acid-washed tees, heavyweight hoodies, five-panel caps, and a flying-duck logo that channels vintage Americana more than any country club.

The Target Practice Tee ($60) and Golf Company Tee ($55) are the entry points — graphic-heavy, built on premium blanks, designed to be worn as much off the course as on it. The Birds Dad Hat ($50) and Target Practice Zip Hoodie ($150) round out a tight catalog that feels more tackle shop than fairway. Merrill is making golf apparel for people who fish, hunt, and happen to play golf — and it turns out that audience is bigger than anyone expected.

The As Seen On roster runs from MLB — Cody Bellinger, Jasson Domínguez, Merrill Kelly, Austin Pope — to Lexie Hull of the Indiana Fever and NFL veterans C.J. Mosley and Tyron Smith. But the brand still feels like it belongs to the weekend golfer.

The credential that matters: an adidas Golf ANTi Gazelle G at 22,000, and shelf space at HBX and at Badlands in New Jersey — the shop that also carries Students and Merrill. When American buyers import you, you are not a local curiosity.

Badlands in Atlantic Highlands, New Jersey is the most useful single stockist — it carries ANTi, Students and Merrill among others. Students is also at Bodega, HBX and Culture Kings, and ANTi is at HBX. Metalwood, Malbon and Casualist are largely direct.

metalwood-studio.name: Metalwood Studio
src: Metalwood Studio is what happens when skate graphics and indie brand culture crash into golf — and nobody apologizes for it. Based on medieval heraldry and industrial signage, the design language is unlike anything else in the space. The Tri-Metal Tee at $54 is the entry point. The Bomber Jacket at $228 and Mechanic Jacket at $278 are the statement pieces.

Beyond the current adidas partnership, Metalwood Studio has collaborated with FootJoy on a golf sneaker, KEEN on a footwear capsule, Maxfli on a golden-era collection, Garrett Leight on eyewear, American Express and Hypebeast on an exclusive capsule, and Oakley on a 2025 Pro M Frame reissue. Nearly all collaboration pieces sold out.

Metalwood Studio is a Los Angeles golf and lifestyle brand built as an ode to golf in the 1990s and early 2000s — the era when persimmon gave way to metal woods, sleeves ran to the elbow, and pleats were everywhere. Founder Cole Young calls the lane it occupies 'a subculture of a subculture of a subculture': high-end yet unassuming, vintage yet never been done, rooted in golf yet often about everything around it.

Metalwood Studio. It is unambiguously streetwear and it had a landmark year — a first golf capsule with adidas Originals in February, and the Sportocasin with G.H.BASS in August. Founder Cole Young still runs it, and the entry price is a $62 tee.

The lineup opens with Metalwood Studio 's adidas MC70 — a Predator upper on a golf chassis — and runs through Quiet Golf 's Samba, Eastside Golf's Jordan AJ1 Low, Malbon's in-house Tour 1, and three Nike retros that belong on a course as much as they do on concrete. PAYNTR shows up three times through collabs with Students Golf , Sugarloaf Social Club , and Vessel — each one engineered differently, each one carrying a different brand's DNA. Thirteen shoes, thirteen stories, $125 to $250.

This is 15 picks from 15 brands. The range runs from the $16 Metalwood Studio Oval Logo Crew to the $39 Whim Golf Featherweight Merino, knit from USA-grown wool in North Carolina. In between: ALD Golf's performance ankle that sells out in minutes, Sugarloaf Social Club 's Made-in-USA arrow socks, and Gumtree Golf's mismatched Flora & Fauna prints. midiron.name: Midiron
src: Midiron writes better product copy than anyone else in golf and will not tell you who is doing it. There is no founder name on the site, no photograph and no byline on any of the writing. On a product page for a sold-out cap, in lowercase and unsigned, is this:

Six of the nine products sign off Golf Apparel Research approved, which reads like third-party validation and is not. Golf Apparel Research is Midiron's own house descriptor, and the line sits at the bottom of the spec list, straight after custom Midiron branded trims , like any other feature. They are approving themselves, on purpose, with a straight face. Nothing else on the site carries a signature either, so a house descriptor standing in for an authority fits the pattern.

Six caps A$69 (about US$49) Caps are the brand and have been since December 2025. Most run cotton twill on an unstructured five-panel with a strap back, and most sign off Golf Apparel Research approved — Midiron approving itself. Three of the six are already gone.

Midiron does not say, and that appears to be deliberate. There is no founder name anywhere on the site and no signature on any of the writing — including the lowercase, first-person story about a grandad's hand-me-down Titleist cap that is the most personal thing on the site. What they do publish is that the brand is Australian: 100% Australian owned, independent Australian business, run out of Sydney. No interviews with the founders have been published anywhere.

It means Midiron approves of Midiron. Engineered for the course, built for everything after. It appears in the spec list on each product page alongside genuine details like mesh internal binding, which is the joke. Three one-off caps, released in July 2026 and gone immediately. Midiron sourced vintage Titleist caps and sent them to Oxy Customs, a Melbourne screen-printing and garment-rework studio, to be reworked. It is the only outside collaboration the brand has done. The reason given is the closest thing to a mission statement they have published: recreating the feeling of being handed a cap by a grandparent, for anyone who gets it.

mogshade.name: Mogshade
src: Mogshade makes golf headcovers by hand in Portugal, and the name tells you everything about the sensibility: it comes from an old English dialect word for the play of light and shadow — sun filtering through leaves onto the course. The whole operation runs on what the brand calls ethical circularity. Everything is made to order (current lead time is about three weeks), which means no overproduction, and the fabrics are natural, recycled, upcycled, offcut, or deadstock — including rescued wool from the Serra da Estrela mountain factories that anchors the Re.Weave and Churra collections. Every piece is slightly different because the fabric was never mass-produced; what you get is what's left from the loom.

The other thing that sets Mogshade apart is how much company it keeps. For a one-workshop operation, the collab sheet reads like a map of independent golf: an artist series with Fabricaal that turned headcovers into canvases, a capsule with IGG that sold through in weeks, Projeto Serra — a tribute to the brand's home mountains, down to the "Ovelha Preta" black-sheep cover — and an "On Set with Manors " edit curated with the London golfwear brand. Add the Depeche Golf magazine bundle, the Ocean Bottle, a Fiumani cap, and the early Parmore run that was capped at 50 pieces, and you get the picture: almost everything they touch disappears. There's also a custom-made program if you want a cover built to your spec from whatever's on the shelf that month.

Mogshade comes from an old English dialect word describing the interplay of light and shadow - like sunlight filtering through leaves and branches onto the course. The brand chose it to capture those quiet moments on a golf course, and its woven patterns play on the same idea.

morning-people-clothiers.name: Morning People Clothiers
src: Morning People Clothiers was built by former collegiate golfers who turned professional and kept asking the same question: why does golf apparel feel like it's made for a billboard instead of a round? Their answer is a five-piece collection that strips out the noise — no loud patterns, no synthetic sheen, no billowy silhouettes — and replaces it with fabric you actually want against your skin at 7 a.m.

odd-ritual.name: Odd Ritual
src: Odd Ritual Golf was born in Cape Town because the founders couldn't find a local golf brand that spoke to them. The culture felt stiff, narrow, exclusionary — a game wrapped in rules about who could play and what they had to wear to do it. So they built something different. Named after the small personal habits every golfer has before a shot — the waggle, the alignment check, the ball mark tap — Odd Ritual is what happens when golf culture gets rewritten from the Southern Hemisphere.

Revisited, August 2026: when we first covered Odd Ritual it was a polos-tees-and-caps brand. Collection 03 changes that. The new range is a full wardrobe — their first Pleated Daily Trouser in 235gsm cotton twill, The Caddie Jacket with washed cotton lining and brass press studs, pigment-washed heavyweight crewnecks, and a 1990s Heritage Polo in 200gsm pique with contrast nylon collar and cuffs. All of it shot on-model in their Cape Town studio, all of it still locally made. Prices now run from R 200 (~$11) for socks to R 3,200 (~$176) for the Caddie Jacket. Off the course, the brand keeps building: their own Odd Folk Invitational golf day, and a website good enough to win Awwwards Site of the Day. This is Cape Town golf culture, built for the course and the community around it.

Odd Ritual is a golf and lifestyle brand from Cape Town, South Africa. The founders started it because they couldn't find a local golf brand that spoke to them — the culture around the game felt stiff, narrow, and exclusionary. Their answer is a brand built on the back of tradition for people who love the game but want to feel like themselves on the course. In their words: less rigid, more real.

The Odd Folk Invitational is Odd Ritual's own golf day — billed as 'not your average golf day' — hosted by the Odd Ritual collective at Royal Durban Golf Club in July 2026, with backing from names like Takomo Golf, New Balance, and Wunderpar. It's the brand's community pillar in action: golf as a gathering, not a gate.

olydoe.name: Olydoe
src: Scott Matthews was an investment banker in New York who couldn't find a cotton polo he wanted to wear on a golf course. src: Drake's first swing at golf came through NOCTA, his Nike sub-label, with a 10-piece recycled-fiber capsule in September 2021. Three years later, he moved the operation under his own roof. OVO Niko, not Drake, is the face of the campaign — photographed in full kit with Jordan golf shoes, an iced-out Rolex, and a cigar. public-drip.name: Public Drip
src: Neil Tan rediscovered golf at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx in 2020, and the result is Public Drip — a label built for the golfers who grew up on public courses, not private ones. Brooklyn-based, streetwear-rooted, and already making noise with a Hypebeast feature, a Cleeks GC collab, and a LINKS Magazine nod as one of 2026's brands to watch.

The owl crest, the QG monogram, the pennant flag: every detail is intentional without being loud.

Quiet Golf is a Southern California golf brand built on restraint — muted palettes, minimalist design, and the idea of golf as somewhere you go to disconnect. In the founders' words: less performance, more presence. The range runs from supima polos and cashmere knits to needlepoint belts and pennant headcovers.
Christion Lennon — who launched the fashion label Museum of Peace & Quiet in 2019 — co-founded Quiet Golf with brothers Raul and Diego Diaz, carrying the same restrained sensibility into golf.

The flagship opened in 2023 in Costa Mesa, Orange County: white stucco outside, four skylights inside, a Foresight simulator, a custom oak shadowbox for the headcover range, and a locker room with tartan carpet and a tournament-style QUIET PLEASE sign.

In October 2024 Quiet Golf closed a seed round led by Old Tom Capital. Asked what he's most protective of as the brand grows, co-founder Diego Diaz answered: 'The pace... If we lose that, we lose the whole point.'

A golf version of the adidas Samba built with Quiet Golf — one of the brand's most sought-after releases, now sold out. Other collabs include hand-forged ball markers with Seamus Golf and needlepoint belts with Smathers & Branson.

src: Erik Anders Lang's first round of golf was December 12, 2011. He was almost 30, a photographer and music video director who'd worked with David LaChapelle and directed for Pharrell. He didn't identify with what seemed to be a sport for conservative White guys. So in 2017, he and co-founder Evan Roosevelt created Random Golf Club — The Global Community of Local Golfers — and set out to change who golf is for.
Random Golf Club’s podcast, released every Monday, with more than 350 episodes recorded completely unedited.

I didn't know a single person when I pulled up to Rodeo Dunes. Seventy-two golfers from across the country, all Random Golf Club members, all here for The Great Divide — a three-round elimination event on one of the newest and most talked-about courses in America. By the time I left, I had a group chat with 15 new people and a very different understanding of what golf can feel like when you're fully locked in.

Random Golf Club was founded in 2017 by Erik Anders Lang — filmmaker, photographer, late-to-golf convert who didn't see himself in the sport and decided to build a version of it he recognized. RGC now has 30,000 members across 140 chapters worldwide. The Great Divide was one of their signature events: competitive enough to matter, casual enough that nobody's checking your handicap card at dinner.

Random Golf Club runs an Australia trip, and no other golf media or apparel brand in the world does. The rest of the field sits it out: No Laying Up, Fried Egg, The Golfer's Journal, Bob Does Sports, Good Good, Skratch, and a dozen clothing labels from Manors to Malbon to Eastside. Fried Egg has a deposit system and a calendar published a year ahead, and points its entire international programme at Britain and Ireland. That leaves a hole in the market, and for now one fourteen-person van tour is filling it.

rouqe-golf.name: Rouqe Golf
src: Rouqe Golf does 1974 club-pro styling better than any label its size, and the proof is which pieces are missing. The burgundy and cream rugby stripe has sold out. Twelve of the twenty-one pieces in the men's collection are gone, and the loudest ones went first, which tells you more about the brand than a fabric spec would.

The photography is the other thing. Rouqe shoots two ways: hard-lit studio portraits against black and deep maroon, styled closer to a streetwear campaign than a golf catalogue, and on-course work at golden hour on a dry mountain course with a lake in the middle distance. Every image on the site is the brand's own, and it carries more atmosphere than labels ten times the size manage.

What Rouqe will not tell you is who runs it. There is no About page, and the URL returns a 404. No founder is named on the store or in any interview, and the domain registration is privacy-shielded. The one person publicly attached to the brand is Marko Mijaljevic, its Head of Design, credited with the SS25 collection. The domain was registered in spring 2023, which dates the shopfront rather than the company. For a label whose whole pitch is a point of view, the anonymity is a strange choice, and the clothes are good enough that it is the only thing holding the story back.

A direct-to-consumer golf apparel label selling polos, mock necks, tees, skorts, dresses, knit sweaters, hats, headcovers and accessories through its own Shopify store at rouqegolf.com. The storefront defaults to Canada and prices in Canadian dollars. The legal name appears as Rouqe Golf Inc.

scotch-and-skins.name: Scotch & Skins
src: No. Every pair in this edit ships bare; the tube-and-rods sets are the fiberglass ones from Tour Sticks, SuperStroke and the big brands. Scotch & Skins makes a matching leather cover but it is sold out, and Hazy sells a see-through leather cover for $60.

scotsticks.name: ScotSticks
src: Ash. ScotSticks makes the case that ash was golf's original wood before hickory crossed from America, and cuts its sticks from it in Scotland. Ekorre goes further and laminates six strips of Swedish ash into a hexagon, the way a split-cane fishing rod is made, so the stick flexes and returns straight.

The details that differ. Length runs 42 to 45 inches; Hickory & Heath picked 43 so the sticks sit below the woods in the bag. Ends are either capped — bronze at Scotch & Skins, brass at Hazy, tack caps at Beavertail, nail caps at BubbaWhips — or bare and chamfered, as ScotSticks and Ekorre prefer. Almost everyone engraves, and about half will paint your colours to order.

Because they are made and sold from there. ScotSticks lists at 51 and ships worldwide with a three-week lead; Ekorre lists at 2,400 kr from Sigtuna. Both note that import duties outside their region are paid by the buyer, so the dollar figures in this post are approximate.

seamus.name: Seamus Golf
src: Seamus turns the headcover into the most personal object in the bag, in registered Irish tartans and licensed Pendleton wool, and the company started with one that was falling apart. Akbar Chisti's father had given him a wool cover from a famous links club, Royal Troon by the company's own telling, and it had worn through. His wife Megan was a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills, so in 2011 she remade it from fabric remnants, sewed a few more for his golf group, and then the two of them were running a company out of their garage. It is named after their Irish Terrier, Seamus O'Reily, and you pronounce it SHAY-mus.

Two things make Seamus more than a nice accessories company. The first is the 2016 Ryder Cup, when Matt Kuchar commissioned personalized American flag covers for the entire U.S. team: thirteen hand-cut stripes, fifty embroidered stars, each one sewn in Oregon. The second is the blacksmith. The Hand Forged line of markers, pitch tools and money clips is hammered rather than cast, by a smith in Portland who now does about ninety per cent of his business with Seamus. The USGA lets them set up and hammer markers on-site at U.S. Open merchandise pavilions, where the brand has sold every year since Chambers Bay in 2015.

At the 2016 Ryder Cup, Matt Kuchar commissioned personalized American flag covers for the entire U.S. team — thirteen hand-cut stripes and fifty embroidered stars each. Kuchar also carried Seamus at the 2016 Olympics, and Bill Murray used one in the Ryder Cup celebrity match. The USA Wool "Patriot" cover in the standing line descends from that commission.

The metal pieces — ball markers, pitch tools, money clips, bag tags — are hand-hammered by the brand's blacksmith in Portland, who now does roughly ninety per cent of his work for Seamus. They are not cast or poured, each comes out slightly different, and hand-stamped personalization up to five characters is free.
The company is named after the founders' Irish Terrier, Seamus O'Reily. It is pronounced SHAY-mus.

Akbar Chisti caddied at Bandon Dunes in college, and the resort placed the brand's first wholesale order — Seamus credits it with getting the company off the ground. Megan quit her Pendleton job shortly after. The pro shops there still carry a dedicated Seamus line.

sentinel-golf.name: Sentinel Golf
src: Sentinel Golf is a product design lab in Minneapolis that makes golf equipment the way an outdoor brand makes a tent. Founder John Mooty runs it on a limited pre-order model — a window opens, you buy or you miss it, and there are no restocks and no discounts — and spends the rest of his time convincing manufacturers outside the game to take a job in it. A Danish tannery. A Nashville chair company. A Brooklyn machine shop. Tent-pole engineers in South Korea. The catalog reads like a list of favors called in.

The reference point is not golf at all; it is the Boundary Waters, the million-acre stretch of protected Minnesota wilderness where you camp, canoe and fish all day with no cell service and can drink the water under your canoe. Mooty built the Basecamp series to hold that feeling inside a golf trip, and the second Basecamp capsule was shot at Sand Valley across three days of camping, fishing and golf on one itinerary. It is why the writer Michael Williams called Sentinel an American Snow Peak, but for golf.

Which makes it a brand for a fairly specific reader: the walker who cares where the fabric was woven, who would rather own four objects for a decade than forty for a season, and who is not put off by an eight-week wait or a bag that costs more than a driver. Prices run from a $30 sock to a $2,900 dome tent. The sold-out archive is longer than the live shop, and that is the point — 112 of the 196 things Sentinel has made are already gone.
Bags first. Sentinel started by rebuilding somebody else's masterpiece in materials nobody had brought to golf, and the carry line is still where the brand argues hardest.
One interview exists. Every quote below is verbatim from The Old Ghosts, Sentinel: Beyond the Green, by Michael Williams, 9 December 2025.

Sentinel Golf is the work of John Mooty, who runs the brand out of Minneapolis. He built it as a product design lab rather than a traditional golf company — a way to experiment, discover, and reimagine, pulling in manufacturers from outside the golf world to make things golf has either never seen or long forgotten.

siegelman-stable.name: Siegelman Stable
src: Siegelman Stable started the way a lot of great brands do — with family history and $600. Max Siegelman's father, Robbie, founded Siegelman Racing Stable in 1982 and spent decades training harness racehorses. Robbie also created equine therapy programs for cancer patients at Hackensack Hospital and inner-city kids from Newark. When the pandemic shut everything down, Max printed hats stamped with the family's horse-and-sulky logo, shipped them to the NBA Bubble, and watched the brand take off from there.

Beyond golf, Siegelman Stable has collaborated with the Knicks, Mets, Yankees, Rangers, Tottenham Hotspur, Prince Tennis, Ford, the Indy 500, Don Julio, and the Muhammad Ali Estate. A portion of all proceeds still goes to equine therapy programs — the same work Robbie started 40 years ago. This is a family-owned brand with substance behind the logo.

Max Siegelman's first job was caddying. Five years carrying bags before he took $600, printed hats during the pandemic, shipped them to the NBA Bubble, and built Siegelman Stable into a NYC luxury streetwear brand that's collaborated with the Knicks, Mets, Yankees, Prince Tennis, Ford, the Muhammad Ali estate, and Don Julio. The brand's DNA is harness racing — Max's father Robbie founded Siegelman Racing Stable in 1982, and the original stable logo is still the centerpiece. Now, with "Harness the Drive," the golf course gets its turn.

sierra-madre.name: Sierra Madre Golf
src: Several, and in more categories than people expect. Clubs and metal: Artisan Golf and P53 in Fort Worth, Piretti in Spring, Edison Golf in Rockport, Lamb Crafted in Plano. Sierra Madre Golf in Austin, founded by Bonny Riddle and Michelle Anderson, is the most established — built-in bras, functional pockets, and an elastic glove loop on the All Square Skort, now stocked in select Golf Galaxy locations. src: What the independents sell splits two ways. RIPIT and Stick Grips work on the full-swing set and treat the grip as a surface to print on, in limited art series and monogram repeats. students-golf.name: Students Golf
src: Students Golf doesn't look like any other golf brand — and that's the point. Founded in 2022 under the tagline For Golfers Who Study The Game,' the label filters streetwear, academic culture, and vintage Americana through a golf lens. Everything borrows from campus life: the Calculus pants, the Librarian polo, the 1st String sweater. Even the internal line is called Course Studies Division.' It's golf apparel designed by people who grew up on skate videos and college football Saturdays, not country club verandas.

The catalog runs deep — 500+ SKUs across polos, pants, shorts, outerwear, hats, headcovers, and accessories. We pulled 18 pieces that represent the full range of what Students does. The Calculus Baggy Pleated Pants are the signature — oversized, carabiner-clipped, built from a custom trico-rayon-spandex blend. The Librarian Polo anchors the performance side with micro-waffle texture and UV protection. The hats and headcovers round it out. Everything ships free in the U.S.

Students Golf 's Draft Blade is the $50 entry point — clean, magnetic, Texas-made. From there it escalates: Fyfe Golf 's Gamekeeper out of Scotland, Gibbons Handmade's Bears Blade, Seamus Golf including a Pendleton collab, and Dormie Workshop's Chevron Atlantic XL at the top. Sunday Rolls, Fried Egg, Winston Collection, Smathers & Branson — all doing their own thing. The common thread is craft. Small-batch, made by people who care about leather, lining, and the snap of a magnetic closure. $50 to $150, all personality.

Malbon covers the range from a clean $58 script logo to the reversible Velasco at $88. Students Golf went full boonie with a screen-printed marble camo that shouldn't work but does. And Birds of Condor — the Australian brand that treats golf hats like an art form — brings the Swing Kings reversible, a corduroy Rage, and the Fore Tiger.

Camo on the course used to mean one thing — the guy who just came from the deer stand. Now it means Realtree collabs with Students Golf , Mossy Oak × Sunday Golf bags, leather headcovers hand-sewn in woodland patterns, and tiger-stripe polos from Devereux that have no interest in blending in. The golf world caught on: camo isn't hiding. It's a print. A texture. A vibe.

sugarloaf-social-club.name: Sugarloaf Social Club
src: Sugarloaf Social Club runs the widest price range in independent golf and holds a single point of view across all of it. The catalogue reaches from a MacKenzie sailcloth bag at $1,400 down to a paper fan at $14, and both read as the same company. It started as a group chat. A few college roommates were graduating in 2011 and wanted somewhere to keep talking about golf, so they named the thread after the course they had spent four years on. The chat became an annual trip, and the trip became an Instagram account that at one point had more followers than Golf Digest. Ian Gilley filed the LLC in 2017 and has described the sequence as a happy little accident.

Sugarloaf Social Club is a subsidiary of Pro Shop, Inc., the golf media company founded by Chad Mumm and Joe Purzycki that raised roughly $20 million from the PGA Tour and Powerhouse Capital. Pro Shop also owns Skratch and GolfWRX. Skratch discloses the shared ownership in its own coverage of the brand.

Eastside Golf's Core Fleece Swingman sets the tone at ~$88 — premium cotton, Swingman embroidery, streetwear DNA. From there, Gumtree Golf goes heavyweight at $145, Malbon pushes into the $185 range with the Safety Buckets Fesque, and Casualist keeps it understated at ~$85. Brands like Sounder, Sugarloaf Social Club , and Jones Golf Bags fill the middle. Whether you need a layer for early morning tee times or a post-round pullover that doesn't scream "I just played 18," the edit covers it.

Rain gear used to mean one thing: a shapeless pullover that made you look like a crossing guard and swung like a straightjacket. That era is over. The waterproof golf market in 2026 runs from $20 snap-on bag covers to $402 Pertex Shield Pro jackets with 30,000mm waterproof ratings — and the best options aren't always the most expensive ones. Sun Mountain's Monsoon delivers 15K waterproof protection for $100. Sugarloaf Social Club built an umbrella that handles 55mph Texas thunderstorms. KJUS engineered a bucket hat from 100% recycled polyester with sealed seams and a drawcord system.

Sugarloaf Social Club's Summer Sailing drop is eight pieces that pull from the same nautical DNA — decommissioned sailcloth turned into one-of-a-kind MacKenzie golf bags, suede boat shoes that work on the dock or the clubhouse patio, and accessories that tie the whole thing together. It's a tight collection with a clear point of view: the overlap between sailing culture and golf culture is bigger than most people think, and SSC is leaning all the way in.

Sugarloaf Social Club and Byrdie Golf went to the Bahamas, shot a lookbook, and came back with a nine-piece collab that blurs the line between resort wear and golf gear. The whole collection is built around terry cloth — Cabana Shirt, Anorak, Short, and Mini Skirt, all in bottle green and sand stripes.

sun-mountain.name: Sun Mountain
src: Sun Mountain invented the bag with legs, and four decades on it still makes the lightest way to walk a golf course. In 1981 a club pro named Rick Reimers quit his job in Northern California and got in the car to drive north to Montana, to ski and think. The car radio was broken, so he spent the whole drive designing a golf bag in his head. What came out the other end was a nylon carry bag that weighed less than half what the leather and vinyl bags of the day weighed.

That was the BACK 9, and it was more interesting than it was successful. The FRONT 9 arrived in 1984 with a moulded top and bottom, sold properly, and became the shape every other carry bag copied. It also earned Sun Mountain the job of building the L8 bag for Ping, which put a Missoula startup in the position of manufacturing for one of golf's giants.

Then, in 1986, they put legs on it. The Eclipse is the bag Sun Mountain is credited with inventing, and its patented stand mechanism is now hinged onto almost every carry bag in the game. They ran the same trick twice more. The Speed Cart in 1999 folded down small enough that people bought one, and a walking-cart category appeared where there had not been one. The ClubGlider in 2008 put retractable legs on a travel bag, so an airport stopped being a workout.

Here is the part that gets left out. Reimers ran the company for 41 years as founder, director and sole shareholder, with no partners, no investors and no board. In March 2022 he sold Sun Mountain Sports to Solace Capital Partners, a Los Angeles private equity firm, and kept the scooter business. The bags are still assembled in Missoula, which remains unusual for the category. The fabrics come from Asia, and the company says assembled in the USA rather than made, which is the honest version.

The line runs across four categories: bags from the $224 Eclipse up to a $1,200 leather stand bag, push carts, travel covers, and small goods down to a $35 headcover. Three of those four are categories Sun Mountain either created or reshaped, which is a strange thing to say about the sensible default.

Three picks $75 $330 Sun Mountain did to walking carts in 1999 what it had done to bags in 1986. The Speed Cart folded down small enough that people actually bought one, and a category appeared where there had not been one.
